demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Mateo is a 22-year-old HVAC technician who came to treatment months after an on-the-job accident in which a coworker was seriously injured. He had been helping move a heavy unit into place in a cramped mechanical room above a restaurant kitchen. He remembers the heat, the metallic smell, and the stale odor of grease rising through the vents. In a tight moment, when everyone was repositioning at once, he shifted his grip and called out too late. The unit slipped and pinned the other man badly. Mateo still speaks about that instant as if it happened in a gap outside ordinary time: he can describe the angle of the machine and the smell in the room with painful clarity, but the memory itself feels strangely unreal, as though it belongs to someone else and not to him.

In the days that followed, what settled most heavily was not only the image of the accident but his conviction that he had failed in a way he could never undo. He had come to believe he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He replayed whether he should have braced sooner, shouted louder, noticed the shift earlier. Alongside that guilt was a new distrust of himself at the most basic level. His hands, his timing, his reflexes no longer felt dependable; he was certain his own body had proven unreliable. When he looked at himself now, he felt unrecognizable, as if the easygoing young man he had been before the accident had been replaced by someone weaker and dangerous.

Those beliefs began to shape how the memory lived in him. Because he was so convinced that his failure said something permanent about who he was, the accident did not sit in the past. It burst into his mind without permission while he was driving, eating, or trying to fall asleep. Sometimes when he thought of that mechanical room he could smell it again immediately—the hot metal, oil, grease, and trapped air—so vividly that he would look around as if he had somehow been pulled back there. The memory’s intrusiveness seemed to confirm his worst ideas about himself: that he was no longer in charge of his own mind or even fully himself.

From there, Mateo began trying to manage his days in ways that felt sensible to him. He avoided dates connected to the accident and became watchful as those calendar days approached. He also started steering away from anything he thought might be stressful, turning down jobs that seemed complicated or unpredictable and lingering only in a few places that felt controlled and familiar—his apartment, his mother’s kitchen, one corner of the workshop. He spent long stretches going over the accident detail by detail, convinced that if he analyzed it enough he might finally find the exact moment he should have prevented it. In practice, these habits deepened the same beliefs that had given rise to them. The more he withdrew from pressure and confined himself to “safe” places, the more fragile and changed he felt; the more he reviewed the scene, the more certain he became that the person he was now was someone he did not recognize and could not trust.

At work, this has become especially clear. HVAC service often means entering quiet basements, empty hallways, and sealed utility spaces before a system kicks on. Mateo has found that unusual silence now makes his body tense immediately, as if danger is about to break through it. In those still moments, his chest tightens, his hands sweat, and he feels a jolt run through him before he can think. A silent service corridor or the stale smell from a vent can bring the accident back at full force, and once the memory forces its way in, his sense of danger spikes further. He has started hanging back on calls, letting others enter first, and avoiding the more stressful jobs entirely. His supervisor has noticed that he is less willing to take assignments alone.

That narrowing of his world has fed the fear. Because he keeps himself to a limited set of places and avoids strain wherever possible, more and more settings now feel unsafe by contrast. Silence is no longer just silence; it feels like the second before something goes wrong. When his body reacts strongly to a reminder, he takes that as proof that he really is no longer reliable. And when he is on edge like that, the memory comes more easily again—the smell, the image, the sickening suspended second before impact—tightening the sense that he cannot get out of what happened.

He finally sought help after realizing he was considering leaving HVAC altogether, not because he wanted a different future but because he no longer believed he could trust himself around other people’s safety. What frightened him most was the thought that this was now his permanent self: a man who could not handle stress, could not trust his own body, and could never stop the accident from happening in his mind. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might find some way to feel like himself again and to be in a workroom without waiting for disaster.
